comments.author: tptacek
comments.text: This is the single most important attack vector for SAAS companies. It has been for a long time --- this is the standard fact pattern for every SAAS breach --- but much more so today. As the number of employees grow, the likelihood that one of their laptops will get compromised approaches 1. When that happens, the attacker will be able to push code to Github, and if that code gets deployed, you're owned. In 1Password's case, the absolute worst-case catastrophe is mitigated by the fact that customers retain custody of their unlocking secrets; 1Password (at least in the normal product flows) simply doesn't hold it. But an attack like this implicates every catastrophe short of that worst case. Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue. You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model). You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security. So the question then becomes: what is review? It's not what r/programming assumes it is; you almost certainly can't literally have a team of people line-by-line reviewing PRs anymore, at least not across the whole codebase (you can and should probably do a threat model for your codebase and institute stuff like that on a case-by-case basis, though). What you can realistically expect to review for is change provenance; a human developer signoff of some sort. But it's tricky! The attacker owns your email during the window of attack. I think this is a fun problem to noodle on, and someone could probably come up with something here that would make a real difference.

stories.title_en: Nfs2root: A 12-year-old pre-auth remote root in the Linux kernel's NFS server

comments.author: gsich
comments.text: no poc posted

comments.author: rvz
comments.text: Just wow. How was this achieved? Let's see: > Pre-auth heap overflow in the Linux NFS server (nfsd) > Set it to the minimum and every slot's buffer is zero bytes. nfsd4_sequence() then shrinks the reply buffer to that limit before it accepts the slot. Pad the request's tag so the buffer fills right after the SEQUENCE opcode, and the encoder quits without flagging an error. The server believes SEQUENCE succeeded and caches the whole reply, headers and tag included, into a buffer with room for nothing. Then it causes an out-of-bounds crash: >> BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in read_bytes_from_xdr_buf+0x1bc/0x390 >> Write of size 80 at addr ffff888003a549cd >> __asan_memcpy+0x38/0x60 >> read_bytes_from_xdr_buf+0x1bc/0x390 >> nfsd4_sequence_done+0x5b0/0x810 >> nfs4svc_encode_compoundres+0x1bf/0x240 So yet another memory corruption issue that gives the attacker control of the execution and its possible to get root on the system and this is in the kernel itself so "hardening" does not remove the bug. What a disaster.

comments.text: Thankfully no one assumed NFS secure for the public internet anyway so this should be minimally impactful. Also looks like it was patched upstream months ago. Still, just another example of why C code can’t be exposed to the internet.

stories.title_en: The polynomial Hirsch conjecture is false [pdf]
stories.title_ja: The polynomial Hirsch conjecture is false [pdf]

comments.author: Luke2642
comments.text: I always like to try to translate it to a really simple English version: You can represent many problems like logistics with a list of linear requirements so valid combinations form a multi-dimensional geometric shape where every corner of that shape and inside that shape represents a 'valid' but probably not optimal solution, e.g. every package gets delivered by a driver, but not the lowest fuel or time, and 'valid' so no rules are broken, like no driver is scheduled more than >24 hours in one day. Every edge is a single step that changes one variable. It's interesting and useful because surprisingly the representation means the optimal solution will always lie on an outside corner. You generally start somewhere 'warm' and try to get hotter, that's the Simplex algorithm. The polynomial Hirsch conjecture was that the number of steps between any two corners grows polynomially as you add more variables and rules, limiting how many steps you might need to find that optimal corner. Now we know you need more steps. Hope I saved you time/tokens though.

comments.author: GIFtheory
comments.text: For context, this means that there is no polynomial-time simplex algorithm (which is an algorithm for linear programming (optimization)). The original version of the conjecture was an attempt to explain why the simplex method seemed to work surprisingly well in practice, but it was disproved in 2010 (after 50+ years!). This seems like more of a mopping up result.

comments.author: rvprasad
comments.text: While the effort is interesting, I found two issues in the list. First, (.indexOf (seq (byte-array [1 2 3])) 2) fails because byte arrays store bytes and the argument 2 to `.indexOf` is a Long value. Simple type checking (via eyeballing) could have flagged the incorrect usage. I think such exercises can be more helpful if we can reduce the noise. Second, (get "abc" 1.9) fails because `get` coerces the given key to integer in the context of string objects, which makes sense; specifically in the context of weakly typed language. That said, I believe that detailed documentation of the behavior of `get` can help clients just as well as returning `nil` or not-found value. However, we are still left with questions such as "who and where do we draw the line about the dynamism of the language?" and "what is the agreed upon semantics that we are checking against?"

comments.author: martythemaniak
comments.text: I don't think the recent spate of math discoveries should be very surprising. Consider 10 years ago when AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, what was really happening there? You had an very large search space (all possible Go moves) that humans had been navigating by a combination of intuition, trial-and-error and passing knowledge between master-student. Then a program was build that could explore that search space both from existing searches (AlphaGo) and from scratch (AlphaGo Zero), and the program found some interesting results (winning moves no one had thought of before). Today's LLMs are vastly bigger and they operate in an immensely larger search space (all of symbolic representation of the world) using immensely more power, and now they're finding results in that search space that people could not. In both cases, the space-search program needed a way to verify whether its results were valid - the Go board in AlphaGo's case, and Lean in current math work. So it really shouldn't be surprising that the space-searchers found something people either missed or was too big/far away to be accessible (that is, it is unknown whether the current RH proof can be simplified and/or understood like classical human proofs)

comments.author: dintech
comments.text: Interesting for audio nerds: Windows actually has an audio limiter. If you playback audio via loopback shared WASAPI, DirectSound or MME it actually gets compressed very slightly as it nears the peaks. The same does not happen via WASAPI exlcusive or ASIO. Playing loudly mastered audio out of your PC will be very slightly different from the true audio source by about -0.1dbps with the compressor affecting the peaks. It works via audiodg.exe (CAudioLimiter in AudioEng.dlll) on the shared-mode render path after all the streams get mixed, even if there's just one playing currently. This is necessary because two loud signals being mixed together might clip your DAC and that sounds nasty, so it's understandable that it's there. Why would you care though? I was building a audio metering system to monitor audio via loopback and the properties of the audio I played in were being modified by the limiter in these normal modes. Maybe audio purists might not enjoy it either.

That In Real Life We humans are adapted to use sound, not because we find it pleasant but because it tells us something about our environment. comments.author: hunter2_
comments.text: This is really cool. I have a suggestion, though: the samples within a button seem to have several modification types including a pitch shifter. For example, "DOWN4" under the "Multi-sampled sounds" heading sounds nearly a semitone lower than the other DOWN variants. I suggest eliminating all pitch shifting (or at least confining your use to a few cents), leaving only timbre variation. Go nuts creating variation through EQ, distortion, formant shifting, reflections/delay/reverb, etc. but keep the pitch locked. Why? Because the pitch of everything in this world is based on its resonant frequency, which is based on the size of whatever can vibrate, and in the case of a button it's resonating based on the size of the button. Many aspects of the sound would change based on things like how quickly the button is pushed or how much dampening the finger pushing it imparts, but the fundamental pitch is not one of them. When playing a violin, if you move up the fingerboard, the pitch of the string increases. But if instead of playing the string you knock on the body as if knocking on someone's front door, the main pitch of that knocking never changes. The sympathetic vibrations of the strings will have frequencies that vary as the finger position varies, and the brightness and RT60 of the reverberation through the wood will vary from knock to knock, but the fundamental frequency generally excited by the knock only changes if the violin's volumetric size changes, and it never will. Maybe a drum is a better example than a violin, since it's "unpitched" and yet still gets tuned to have some fundamental frequency. Only the noisy stuff varies from hit to hit, and the fundamental frequency does not (until you re-tune, or from temperature/humidity changing).

comments.author: kevinsync
comments.text: I posted this and went to bed, and now figure I probably ought to at least write up some of the actual tech, implementation and features, and there's so much that I don't even know where to begin lol. RCHIVE does indeed use Electron. I know that's probably going to catch a lot of flak, but I chose it intentionally due to things I wanted to do in the UI that, hate to say it, Chromium does out of the box that would become a whole sidequest trying to do in Qt or Swift. The front end is underpinned by a variety of daemons and services written in Rust that handle scan coordination and watching, shared platform primitives, executing copy jobs, handling offline geography, decoding media (using OS-native decoders and handling legacy formats), etc. There are other coordinators and workers in Node as well. Database is SQLite, which manages your catalog and executes searches via regular indexes and FTS5 trigram indexes. There's a whole gang of stuff in there to optimize and facilitate searches based on filename/path substrings, scanned metadata, etc. Will be releasing an update with indexing and searching of actual file contents soon. Different people will use RCHIVE for different purposes: - Search/Find: you can see the most recently-changed files, deep-search across all sources, filter based on a bunch of different parameters, etc. You can get just a list of results, or see everything hierarchically in File Browser. Every file that can generate a preview gets one, and there's contextual clustering that happens where appropriate (ex. RCHIVE looks for evidence in sibling files to make decisions based on consensus, such as "folder with 20 MP3s all tagged appropriately, and a couple stray JPGs of unknown provenance -- these very likely all belong together"). Filters are combinatorial and have their own structured syntax, so you can type them out if you want, or use the UI. Previews show images, animated video frames, rendered PDF pages, etc, so you can zip through a bunch of IMG_0XXX files super fast. There's also a "Mini Mode" that's just a search box, so you can start the app, minimize to system tray, then hotkey to search from any other app. Ctrl-shift-R, type, enter, keyboard search, enter to open. Just as easy as Spotlight et al. - Organize: you can take a massive, disparate catalog and apply Recipes (to filter/reduce the dataset) and Transformations (to group and restructure the file tree) to virtually build an organized filesystem, which you can then simply browse, or copy/move some-or-all of it from its messy origin to a tidy destination (new drive, NAS, whatever) -- both recipes and transformations are JSON, so while RCHIVE ships with a ton of presets, you can write your own to basically do whatever you want. The recipe engine is composible and honestly really neat, because you can end up crafting really specific, reusable combination views of all your shit (which then stay updated if you manually rescan, or turn background scanning on). Tagging is also very comprehensive; descendants inherit them by default, but can disinherit granularly. Makes it really easy to tag large swaths of things from a parent - Copy/Move: granular jobs get created which then are executed via rchive-runner (either on CLI or in-app) -- every individual filesystem action is tracked and able to resume/rerun, so if you're copying 10TB of stuff, your power can go out and you don't have to start over. You can pause and come back days later. Care is taken to ensure that stuff like a file "move" isn't marked complete and source isn't removed until file is copied and verified at the destination (either simple verification, or full SHA256 hash checks if needed) There's all kinds of other random useful stuff in there: - all geo/location functions use H3, GeoNames data, and some custom projections and custom data, all offline/on-device. I handle Earth like a truncated icosahedron at varying levels of resolutions, and it rips through locations by bucketing everything into 3D hexagonal tiles which makes lookups easy and fast - you can take a photo of each source for quick identification (ex. "that yellow thumb drive") -- you just click the source, scan a QR code that pops up with your phone, take the photo with your phone, submit - you can "cold copy" paths/drives without cataloging them, like if you simply want to run a job from point A to B - there's pretty comprehensive keyboard support, complex selections, undo/redo, etc - you can make complex selections and then "isolate" the selection, so you're only working with a chosen subset of your catalog - when scanning files, we also look for duplicates, files that are "broken" (a JPG that's actually MP3 data), etc -- for instance, I had a drive from 2002 that I guess had some bad sectors, and I copied it off back then and have carried it ever since. I didn't realize a few of the photos "copied" but the drive head actually read from another area that had some music files, and only found out when they got surfaced during an RCHIVE scan 24 years later. Long story short, Winamp plays those JPGs just fine lol - I also integrated PairDrop into it, so you can pretty easily fire off files or selections of files from inside the app directly to your phone or other devices Anyways, that's just a bit more background about what it all is. Happy to discuss further if anybody has any thoughts or questions!

comments.author: anothaway
comments.text: Something really bothers me about the "it's just another higher-level abstraction" argument but I can't quite nail down what. Using an LLM is a completely different experience from moving to assembler to C, or C to Javascript. The nature of the activity you are performing in those transitions in the same, moving to an LLM is not. Even if you are writing in Javascript, you are still modelling a problem on to some representation in code. The only thing that is abstracted from you is memory management, a technical detail. With an LLM you don't model the problem at all, you let something else do it. Moving from an low-code app builder to an LLM is a higher level of abstraction. Moving from writing code yourself to having an LLM write it is something different entirely. (Though the author seems to be advocating against that style of usage, which I agree with.)

On the one hand, you have languages like C++ and Swift which have construction as a first-class concept, with tons of rules you need to memorize (Swift's "convenience" vs "designated" initializers are a real treat to unpack). Then you have languages like Rust, Go, Zig, etc which don't have them at all, constructors are just static functions in the namespace of the type, which return an instance of that type. For the life of me I've never understood why you'd want the former. I'm sure there's a reason, but I never miss it when using languages in the latter category. The explanation you typically hear is about OO and inheritance, but I don't buy it: If Animal had a ::new() that initialized private state, Cow could have a ::new() too that could call Animal::new() if it wanted, then do further initialization, etc... comments.text: The example is pretty contrived because in practice you'd want to zero-initialize the members in the default constructor anyway. struct span { const char *p = nullptr; size_t len = 0; span() = default; // or span() {} span(const char *s, size_t n) : p(s), len(n) {} }; In that case, there is no difference between span s; and span s{}; There are only few use cases where you want a default constructor that does not initialize its members. One example are wrappers around primitive types where you want to closely preserve the original semantics. Whether that's a good idea in the first place really depends on the use case. For example, std::atomic used to default-initialize the underlying value, which led to many bugs in user code. Since C++20 std::atomic uses value-initialization. See https://cplusplus.github.io/LWG/issue2334 . On the one hand, std::atomic is now safer to use, on the other hand, it is not an implicit-lifetime-type anymore, which means you can't put it in shared memory without UB... Another example is glm::vec, which has actually hit me a few times in my own code. At least they recognized the issue and allowed to override the default behavior with the GLM_FORCE_CTOR_INIT define.

comments.author: amluto
comments.text: This shared LV cache thing is, in my mind, ridiculous. Web browser developers learned, quite a while ago, that caches need to be separated for different origins. Inference servers should add a similar feature: allow API calls to specify cache separation keys that prevent one security context from probing another context’s cache. As for the step size issue, Google recently had a post about producing exactly consistent output across different kernels (specifically by defining a deterministic prefill algorithm and then requiring all kernels to generate results exactly equal to prefilling on the sequence in question). More broadly, I think it’s a bit odd to frame this as “models” communicating. This is software communicating, and the models happen to be running the software.

comments.author: tsimionescu
comments.text: None of the attacks discussed here are realistic in any way. They require a bunch of extremely improbable conditions to hold, and a huge amount of information on the exact details of the hardware and software stack. - the two agents must be aware of each other and must have pre-shared messages to check - they can't spontaneously discover each other and start communicating in this way - they must know the details of the inference server they are running under and its possible kernels and its limits (what is a "short prompt" vs "a long prompt" for this setup) - they must have a way to run at almost the same time - the prefix cache must have little contention so that their blocks can't be evicted (note: the article mostly talks about KV cache, but it's actually the prefix cache that is relevant here) - the models need either (1) direct access to the numerical results of the inference process, instead of the text that vLLM provides, (2) access to the exact responses that a helper model will produce with the short-kernel numerical results vs the long-kernel numerical results; this is the most critical step that is impossible to reproduce on any common kind of deployment - there must not be any other kind of variability in the system (different GPUs, multiple inference servers behind a load balancer, more complex distributed inference setups) The post also mentions all of these limitations, and that the scheme entirely collapses if any of them don't hold. It's a cool idea, but it's a purely theoretical thing that has 0 real-world implications.

comments.author: kgeist
comments.text: If a single vLLM instance handles both prefill and decode without disaggregation, I can think of another way. Alice reads a long document every N seconds to transmit a 1, and does nothing to transmit a 0. Bob, in its own loop, measures the time using bash, generates some random text and writes it to a file, and then checks the time again to estimate its own tokens per second (file length / elapsed time). The trick is that when a vLLM instance handles both prefill and decode, decoding slows down measurably because vLLM has to alternate between prefill and decode phases. It assumes only 2 agents are running, though, but it doesn't require fine-tuning or a second helper model.
